evidence.label: Stable self-similar blowup for a supercritical defocusing Schrödinger equation on the torus

headline: Proves that blowup is stable for a defocusing Schrödinger equation on a 12-dimensional torus, for some large odd power.
scope: The scalar defocusing equation i∂ₜu + Δu = |u|^{p−1}u on the twelve-dimensional torus, for one large odd power p. Data lie in a Sobolev space H^k, k > 8.
plain: The Schrödinger equation describes waves, and the defocusing kind has a force that pushes waves apart. One might expect such waves to stay smooth forever. The paper builds an open set of smooth starting waves that still blow up in finite time. Open means small changes to the start do not stop the blowup. As a result, some random starting waves blow up with positive probability.
doesNot: This does not say which odd power works or give a number for it. It does not claim blowup with probability one, and it treats only dimension twelve.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It gives a stable, open set of blowup data for a scalar defocusing equation, where earlier constructions gave only thinner families of data.

explanation:
Start with the simplest wave: a constant, u = c, spread evenly over the space. The equation here is i∂ₜu + Δu = |u|^{p−1}u. For constant data the derivative term Δu is zero. The solution only turns its phase: u(t) = c·e^{−i|c|^{p−1}t}. Its size |u| stays equal to |c| forever. Nothing blows up. The question is whether a wave that is not flat can concentrate into a point of infinite height.

Here u is a complex wave on the torus. The torus is a box whose opposite faces are glued, so waves leave one side and come back on the other. The symbol Δ is the Laplacian, which spreads the wave out. Defocusing means the right side also pushes the wave apart. Blowup means the solution stops being smooth at some finite time T.

The energy of the wave stays fixed and positive. In twelve dimensions, though, it does not control the smoothness needed to continue the solution[3]. Each power p has a critical smoothness level, d/2 − 2/(p−1). For d = 12 this is 5 when p = 3 and 5.98 when p = 101, far above 1.

Earlier work built blowup in nearby settings. Tao used a specially designed vector system with forcing[4]. Merle, Raphaël, Rodnianski and Szeftel found radial blowup for four pairs of dimension and power, under a stated condition[5]. Cao-Labora, Gómez-Serrano, Shi and Staffilani did the cubic case on an eight-dimensional torus[6]. Those two gave only thin families of starting data. One recent result did not claim an open set of data[7].

The paper claims that for some large odd power, an open set of starting data in a Sobolev space H^k blows up[1]. A Sobolev space measures smoothness through k derivatives. The blowup is self-similar: the spike has width (T−t)^{1/2} and height (T−t)^{−1/(p−1)}[8]. To show the scaling, suppose p were 5. When T − t = 0.0001, the width is 0.01 and the height grows tenfold. Because the set is open, random Gaussian starting data hit it with positive probability[2,9]. The paper does not claim blowup with probability one[10]. The key tool is a limit of very large powers. There, the spike profile has a flat core and a free outer part[11].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has a formal statement of the open blowup set and the Gaussian result. So the paper proves them, as far as the Lean statement matches the paper. Lean gives arbitrarily large odd powers, not every large odd power. No specialist review of the paper is published.
hypeCheck: A major result with a Lean statement of both main claims. The power is not specified, only dimension twelve is treated, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: An equation for a complex wave whose motion depends on the wave's own size.
The nonlinear term pushes the wave apart rather than pulling it together.
A box whose opposite faces are glued, so the space has no edge.
The solution stops being smooth at a finite time, here by growing without bound at a point.
The functions whose first k derivatives have finite total square size.
A set of starting data where every small enough change stays in the set.
The spike keeps the same shape while it narrows and grows by fixed power laws in time.
Random starting waves built from independent bell-curve random numbers, one per frequency.
